section.title: Blessed Is He Who Considers the Poor
section.sectionRationale: The last psalm of Book I, David moves from a beatitude on caring for the poor, to his own prayer for healing under sickness and sin, to the sharpest betrayal in the psalm, a close friend who ate his bread turning against him, a verse Jesus applies directly to Judas. It closes with the doxology that ends Book I of the Psalter.
section.thesis: David's prayer for healing under sickness and sin is deepened by the betrayal of a trusted friend who shared his bread, a wound Jesus takes upon Himself when He identifies Judas's betrayal with this very verse, before the psalm closes in confident praise that opens onto the doxology ending Book I.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the opening beatitude on considering the poor, verses 1-3; David's own prayer for healing amid confessed sin, verses 4-9; the sharp betrayal by a close friend, verse 9's center; and the closing plea and doxology, verses 10-13.

units.label: Blessed is the one who cares for the poor

verses.text: Blessed is the one who cares for the poor; the LORD will deliver him in the day of trouble.
The LORD will protect and preserve him; He will bless him in the land and refuse to surrender him to the will of his foes.
The LORD will sustain him on his bed of illness and restore him from his bed of sickness.

units.label: Heal me, for I have sinned against You

verses.text: I said, "O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against You."
My enemies say with malice: "When will he die and be forgotten?"

My visitor speaks falsehood; he gathers slander in his heart; 
he goes out and spreads it abroad.
All who hate me whisper against me; they imagine the worst for me:
"A vile disease has been poured into him; he will never get up from where he lies!"

units.label: He who shared my bread has lifted his heel against me

verses.text:
Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my {{lechem|bread}}, 
has lifted up his heel against me.

units.label: By this I know that You delight in me

verses.text: But You, O LORD, be gracious to me and raise me up, that I may repay them.
By this I know that You delight in me, for my enemy does not triumph over me.
In my integrity You uphold me and set me in Your presence forever.

Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. 
Amen and Amen.

lechem.gloss: Bread, the staple food of daily life and a symbol of shared table fellowship and covenant trust. Sharing bread implied friendship and loyalty, which makes the betrayal that follows, 'has lifted up his heel against me,' so sharply painful, and why Jesus quotes this exact verse of Judas at the Last Supper's table, John 13:18.

basic.context: The last psalm of Book I opens with a beatitude on the one who cares for the poor, then turns personal, David praying for healing while confessing his own sin, surrounded by enemies who wish for his death and a visitor who spreads slander. At its center falls the psalm's sharpest wound, betrayal by a close, trusted friend who shared his bread, before the psalm turns to confident praise and closes Book I with a doxology.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm should be read as a whole, its opening beatitude on mercy toward the poor is not separate from its plea for personal healing, both flow from the same conviction that the LORD is gracious to those in need, while its central betrayal verse gains its fullest weight only when read alongside Jesus's own use of it.
basic.originalLanguages: Verse 9's betrayal centers on lechem, shared bread, the ordinary sign of table fellowship and covenant loyalty in the ancient world, which is precisely why a friend turning against the one who shared that bread cuts so deeply, and why Jesus applies this verse directly to Judas at the table of the Last Supper.
basic.typology: David's betrayal by a trusted table companion who shared his bread anticipates Christ's betrayal by Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve who shared His table and even His bread at the Last Supper, a connection Jesus Himself draws explicitly.
basic.christ: Jesus quotes this psalm's verse 9 directly and applies it to His own betrayal: 'He who is eating My bread has lifted up his heel against Me,' John 13:18, spoken of Judas at the Last Supper's own table. Where David's betrayal was a bitter but survivable wound, Christ's betrayal by one who shared His bread led to the cross, yet even there God's purposes of salvation were being accomplished, showing this psalm's pattern of suffering unjustly at a friend's hand fulfilled and transformed in the gospel.
basic.god: God is shown as the one who delivers, protects, and sustains those who show mercy to the poor and the sick, who hears honest confession of sin, and whose presence forever, not the absence of betrayal, is what finally upholds the one in integrity.
basic.crossReferences: John 13:18 quotes this exact verse of Judas Iscariot's betrayal of Jesus at the Last Supper. Matthew 25:34-40 develops the opening beatitude's concern for the poor into care shown to Christ Himself in the least of these. Psalm 22 and Psalm 55 share this psalm's theme of betrayal by trusted friends, deepening into Christ's own experience.
basic.oneStory: David's mercy for the poor, honest confession under sickness, and bitter betrayal by a trusted friend who shared his bread anticipate Christ, who showed perfect mercy to the poor, bore sin though sinless, and was betrayed by Judas at His own table, fulfilling this very psalm on the way to the cross and the salvation it accomplished.

context.literary:
Psalm 41 is the last psalm of Book I of the Psalter, and it is built to close a book. It opens, as the whole book opened at Psalm 1:1, with the word 'blessed,' and it ends with a doxology that shuts the collection in the way Psalm 72:18-20, Psalm 89:52 and Psalm 106:48 shut the next three. Between Psalm 1 and Psalm 41 lies the story of a righteous man tried and kept, and this psalm gives that story in small.

Within the psalm the movement is a sandwich. Verses 1 to 3 are a general statement in the third person, promise after promise about the one who deals kindly with the weak. Verse 4 changes to first person prayer, 'I said,' and from verses 4 to 10 the psalmist describes his own case in four steps: his own confession, his enemies' wish, the visitor's slander, and the friend's betrayal. The psalm then turns at verse 10 with the emphatic 'But You, O LORD,' and verses 11 and 12 move to confidence. Verse 13 is the doxology, in a different voice, the voice of the congregation.

The centre of the psalm's argument is the pair of verbs of rising. In verse 8 the enemies say of the sick man 'he will never get up,' and in verse 10 he prays 'raise me up,' the same verb in a different form. The whole psalm is a contest between two statements about the same bed. Alongside this runs the sound play of shalom. The friend of verse 9 is literally the 'man of my peace,' and the psalmist's word for repaying in verse 10 is built on the same root. The betrayal is made more bitter because it comes from one whose name meant wholeness, and the response is left to the root of wholeness, not the root of harm.
context.historical:
The psalm belongs to the world of the sick room in ancient Israel, where a person struck down was surrounded by a kind of ritual visiting. Friends and neighbours were expected to come, and the psalm shows how the visit could be a cover. 'My visitor speaks falsehood,' verse 6, and 'he goes out and spreads it abroad.' A ruler who lay ill was a target for those who wanted his place, and news of his condition was currency. The enemies' question, 'When will he die and be forgotten?' verse 5, in the Hebrew asks when his name will perish, which in Israel was a wish for the end of a house, Deuteronomy 25:6. The whispered word in verse 8, that 'a vile disease has been poured into him,' has the feel of a curse spoken over the sick, or of a diagnosis that says he is finished.

The betrayal of verse 9 belongs to the same setting. To 'eat bread' with a man in the East was to be under his protection and to owe him loyalty, and a betrayal from such a person was a breach of covenant of the deepest kind. The psalm gives no name. Many readers link it to Ahithophel, David's counsellor who went over to Absalom's conspiracy, 2 Samuel 15:12, and who hanged himself when his advice was rejected, 2 Samuel 17:23. Psalm 55:12-14 speaks of a companion and close friend with whom the psalmist shared sweet fellowship and who turned on him, and that psalm is often set beside this one. The psalm itself, however, leaves the man unnamed, and the connection with Ahithophel remains an inference.

The ethics of the opening verses grow out of the covenant's care for the poor. The king of Israel was expected to be the defender of the weak, Psalm 82:3 and Psalm 72:12-14, and to be counted among those who 'considered the poor' was a title of honour for the ruler.
context.canonical:
Psalm 41 opens with the same word that opens Psalm 1, and it belongs to a pattern that frames Book I. Psalm 1:1 says 'Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked,' Psalm 2:12 ends 'Blessed are all who take refuge in Him,' and Psalm 41:1 begins 'Blessed is the one who cares for the poor.' The blessing of the book runs from the man who delights in the Law, to those who take refuge in the Son, to the man who deals gently with the weak. It closes on a doxology that is the same in form as Psalm 72:18-19, 89:52 and 106:48, and Luke's Gospel opens Zechariah's song with these very words, 'Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel,' Luke 1:68.

The theme of mercy to the poor threads through the Law, the Wisdom books and the Gospels. Proverbs says 'Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender,' Proverbs 19:17, and 'whoever is kind to the needy honors Him,' Proverbs 14:31. Jesus says 'Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy,' Matthew 5:7, and says of the least of His brothers, 'you did for Me,' Matthew 25:40.

The betrayal in verse 9 is one of the most followed lines in the psalter. The BSB footnote records that it is cited in John 13:18, where Jesus says 'The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me.' The Gospels report the same scene in Mark 14:18, 'one of you who is eating with Me will betray Me,' and Matthew 26:23. The prayer for healing and for being raised up is echoed in the healing of Psalm 30:2-3, and the confession 'I have sinned against You' comes close to Psalm 51:4. The psalm, in short, gathers the blessings, betrayals and prayers of Book I into a last, honest summary.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm was written to teach a paradox that any believer meets: God's promises are real, and yet the one who trusts them may lie ill and be surrounded by enemies. The author places the beatitude of verses 1 to 3 first, before the trouble, so that the reader reads the trouble in its light. He does not hide that the promises appear to fail. He says 'I said, O LORD, be gracious to me,' verse 4, and shows a man who is not in the position of receiving them, and who asks for grace rather than claiming a reward.

He also meant to tell how to survive a betrayal. The sufferer does not seek revenge in the text as it is spoken; he asks God to raise him up, and his hope rests on a sign, 'By this I know that You delight in me, for my enemy does not triumph over me,' verse 11. The vindication is God's, and it is seen in the outcome.

The last purpose is the doxology. The book of psalms so far has been a long record of trials, and the author closes it with praise in the presence of unfinished business. Praise does not wait until all the enemies are gone. The verse says 'from everlasting to everlasting,' and it thereby sets every particular trouble in the frame of God's endless reign. The double 'Amen' invites the whole congregation to take the psalm's faith as its own.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records a man's experience and gives a set of promises in its first three verses. It is worth noticing what kind of promises they are. They are wisdom statements in the manner of Proverbs, general truths about how God treats those who care for the weak, not guarantees that any given kind act will be repaid with health on a given day. The psalmist himself lies sick in verse 3 and confesses sin in verse 4, and the case of Job and the words of Jesus in John 9:3 forbid a simple system. The passage prescribes the practice of mercy to the poor, and it describes the goodness of God who honours it, without turning kindness into a way to purchase healing.

The wish of verse 10, 'that I may repay them,' is a description of the psalmist's desire and should not be taken as a rule for believers. The New Testament says 'Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath,' Romans 12:19, and Jesus prayed 'Father, forgive them,' Luke 23:34. The right way to read the wish is as the prayer of a king for the restoration of justice, held in check by the rest of Scripture.

The treatment of betrayal is likewise a case study. The psalm describes the pain of it and does not command a particular way to respond, but the example of the psalmist is instructive: he tells God, he asks to be raised, he waits for a sign, and he keeps his praise.

debates.question: How can the psalmist say 'I have sinned against You,' verse 4, and also 'in my integrity You uphold me,' verse 12?

views.label: Integrity means wholehearted loyalty, not sinlessness
views.case: The Hebrew word for integrity describes a person who is whole, undivided in devotion, and it is used of people who clearly still sin, as in the prayers of Psalm 25:21 and Psalm 26:1. The psalmist confesses particular sin and is still a man of integrity in the sense that his heart is with God. That is why he can ask for grace and still be upheld.

views.label: Integrity relative to his accusers
views.case: The psalm's enemies charge him with something that has brought him down, and he can call himself upright in the matter they raise. His confession in verse 4 is to God and covers his general sinfulness, while his integrity in verse 12 refers to the specific charge. Job says something similar in Job 27:5-6.

views.label: Integrity is a gift, seen fully in Christ
views.case: In the light of the whole Bible, no one but Christ has perfect integrity. On this view the psalm looks beyond David to the One whom God can uphold on the ground of His own righteousness, and to those who have His righteousness given to them, 2 Corinthians 5:21.

debates.bearing: The first two views keep the psalm within David's own life, and the third reads it with the whole canon. They agree that confession and integrity are not in conflict: a man may be honestly sorry for his sin and honestly devoted to God, and God upholds him.

debates.question: What is to be made of 'that I may repay them,' verse 10?

views.label: A royal desire for justice, to be read within the covenant
views.case: The psalmist is a king and holds the office of judge. To 'repay' is to set right, and the psalm asks God to raise him so that he may exercise the justice that belongs to his office. The Old Testament often speaks of the Lord's anointed dealing with the wicked, Psalm 2:9 and Psalm 101:8.

views.label: A human desire that the New Testament corrects
views.case: The verb for repay is the word of vengeance and shares the root of shalom, and the wish rings harshly beside Jesus' teaching to love enemies, Matthew 5:44, and Paul's instruction to leave vengeance to God, Romans 12:19-21. The Lord Himself quotes verse 9 in John 13:18 and does not quote verse 10, and He forgives from the cross, Luke 23:34.

debates.bearing: The psalm preserves an honest human wish and does not hide it. Readers are invited to bring such wishes to God, and the fuller revelation of Christ teaches them how to hold them: leave the repayment with God and answer evil with good.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 opens 'Blessed is the one who cares for the poor.' The verb behind 'cares' is maskil, a word for one who acts wisely, considers and gives thought to a matter, and the word for 'poor' is dal, the thin or weak, the one whom Psalm 82:3 tells rulers to defend. The verse thus asks for a thoughtful, discerning attention to the weak, not a passing gift. The person is blessed who thinks about the poor.

Verse 3 says the LORD will 'sustain him on his bed of illness,' and adds a striking clause that the BSB renders 'restore him from his bed of sickness.' The Hebrew says something closer to 'You turn over all his bed in his sickness,' a homely picture of God as a nurse who turns and remakes the sickbed. Verse 4 says 'heal me,' with the noun 'soul' in the Hebrew, so that the prayer is to heal my soul, my whole self, 'for I have sinned against You.' Sin and illness are joined in the one plea.

Verse 5's enemies ask when he will die and his 'name' perish. Verse 6 says the visitor 'speaks falsehood' when he comes to see him, a detail that brings out the deceit of a visit made for spying. Verse 8 calls the thing poured into him 'a vile disease,' but the Hebrew phrase is a thing or word of worthlessness, davar beliyya'al, and it can be read either as a wicked word, a curse, or as a deadly matter. Verse 8 ends 'he will never get up,' and verse 10 answers, 'raise me up,' both from the verb qum. The enemies' prediction and the psalmist's prayer are exact opposites.

Verse 9 is the heart of the psalm. The friend is literally 'the man of my shalom,' ish shelomi, and is one 'whom I trusted' and who 'shared my bread,' the bread being lechem, the ordinary food of the table. He 'has lifted up his heel,' the verb meaning to make great, so that the heel is raised against him, in the Hebrew the noun aqev. That noun is the word for the heel in Genesis 3:15, where the serpent will 'strike his heel,' and it is the root behind the name Jacob, who was born 'grasping Esau's heel,' Genesis 25:26, and who 'cheated' his brother, Genesis 27:36. Whether the psalmist means to echo Genesis is not stated, but the heel is the place of treacherous attack throughout Scripture.

John 13:18 puts it in Greek with a different verb for eating. Where the Greek translation has 'eating,' John writes trogo, the word he uses for eating the bread of life in John 6:54-58. In verse 10 the verb 'repay' is from the root of shalom, and in verse 11 the verb 'delight' is chafets, which appears also in Psalm 40:6, 8 and 14. The psalm ends with the doxology in the words min ha'olam ve'ad ha'olam, 'from everlasting to everlasting,' resembling the word 'forever' of verse 12.

typology.type: The friend who shared the bread and lifted his heel, verse 9
typology.fulfillment: David is betrayed by a trusted friend who ate at his table. Jesus applies the verse to Judas on the night He is betrayed: 'The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me,' John 13:18, and He adds that He tells them beforehand so that they will believe that He is the one, verse 19. The correspondence is exact at the table. The escalation is that the betrayal leads not to a sickbed but to the cross. Judas, like the man who may lie behind the psalm, ended by hanging himself, Matthew 27:5. The type falls short because David's friend betrayed a king, and Judas betrayed the King of kings who knew it in advance.

typology.type: The sick man whom enemies say will not rise, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: His enemies say of him 'he will never get up from where he lies,' and the psalmist prays 'raise me up.' The pattern comes to its fullest in the death of Christ, whom His enemies thought they had finished, and whom God raised on the third day. Peter says 'God raised Him up, releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for Him to be held in its power,' Acts 2:24. The escalation is that the psalmist was raised from a sickbed and Christ from a tomb. The type falls short because David rose to face death again, and Christ rose to die no more.

typology.type: The one who considers the weak, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: The blessed man is the one who thoughtfully cares for the poor. Christ is that man perfectly. He is the King who 'will deliver the needy who cry out,' Psalm 72:12, and He identifies Himself with the least, so that what is done for them is done for Him, Matthew 25:40. Paul says that 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9, so that the poor might be made rich. The type falls short in the fact that the psalm's blessed man is blessed for his kindness, while Christ is the source of blessing for those who have no kindness to offer.

study.christ:
John 13:18 is the plain link between this psalm and Jesus. At the Last Supper He says 'I am not speaking about all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But this is to fulfill the Scripture: The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me.' The BSB footnote to Psalm 41:9 notes the citation. The word 'fulfill' here does not mean that David was speaking only of a future Judas. It means that a pattern in David's life comes to its full form in the life of the Son of David. David was betrayed by a man he trusted, and the greater David is betrayed in the same way, at a table, with bread.

The scene has details that press the link. Jesus tells them 'so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I am He,' John 13:19. He does not treat the betrayal as a disaster that has escaped Him but as a sign that He is who He says. The other Gospels record the identifying detail, 'the one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Me will betray Me,' Matthew 26:23, and 'one of you who is eating with Me,' Mark 14:18. The Lord's own comment shows how He read it, 'The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him, but woe to that man by whom He is betrayed,' Matthew 26:24. The betrayal is written, and the betrayer is still responsible.

Jesus quotes verse 9 and leaves out verse 10. That is instructive. David asks to be raised up 'that I may repay them.' Jesus is raised up, and what He does with His resurrection is to send out the message of forgiveness. The one who prayed 'Father, forgive them,' Luke 23:34, applies the first half of the psalm's betrayal and rejects the psalmist's wish for repayment.

The psalm points to Christ in other ways. The opening beatitude is realised in the One who took up the cause of the weak, and who says that what is done to them is done to Him. The prayer 'raise me up' is answered on the third day, and verse 12, 'You uphold me ... and set me in Your presence forever,' is fulfilled in His session at the right hand, Hebrews 10:12. The confession 'I have sinned against You,' verse 4, is a place where the psalm cannot be put in His mouth, since He had no sin, and yet He took the sin of the confessor.

A caution: the psalm's own picture is of a sick man and a group of enemies, and it is not every line that speaks of Christ. The link the New Testament itself makes is verse 9. The rest reads best as David's prayer, which finds its fullest answer in Christ.
study.god:
The God of Psalm 41 is the God who honours mercy. The first three verses set out a sequence of His actions, that He delivers in the day of trouble, protects and preserves, blesses in the land, refuses to hand the one who has been merciful to his foes, sustains him on his sickbed and remakes his bed. Each verb has the LORD as its subject. The passage says something about God's character as much as about the man: He is on the side of the weak, and He takes the care of the weak as service to Himself, as Proverbs 14:31 says.

He is gracious to a sinner. The psalmist's prayer in verse 4 is 'be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against You,' and the second is nearly the same in verse 10, 'be gracious to me and raise me up.' Grace is asked for on the ground of sin, not of merit. The psalm shows a God who hears prayers that begin with confession, and who does not disqualify a man for having sinned.

He delights in His people. 'By this I know that You delight in me,' verse 11, uses the verb chafets, which in Psalm 40:6 says what God did not delight in, sacrifices, and in Psalm 40:8 says what the psalmist delights in, God's will. Here God's delight has a person as its object. It is a great word to find at the end of the book: the LORD delights in the man who trusts Him, and shows it in the outcome.

He holds the future of the one He upholds. 'You uphold me and set me in Your presence forever,' verse 12. The tenses matter. A man who lies on a sickbed says God will set him before His face 'forever,' a word that reaches past the death his enemies wish on him. The hope goes further than the psalm can spell out, and later Scripture fills it in.

He is the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. The closing doxology takes the psalm's individual trial and places it inside the great story of the covenant people and the everlasting God. The double 'Amen and Amen' is a confession that the one who has done these things is worthy of endless blessing.

For worship, the psalm teaches that the practice of mercy is part of it, that a betrayed person may bring the wound to God, and that praise does not have to wait for the trouble to end. It tells a congregation that the God they sing to has a bias to the poor, and that His delight is what finally holds a person up.

crossReferences.note: Jesus quotes verse 9 of the psalm about Judas at the Last Supper, 'The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me,' and adds that He says it beforehand so that they will believe that He is the one. It is the New Testament's own use of the psalm, and the footnote at Psalm 41:9 points to it.

Jesus says 'The one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Me will betray Me,' and adds that the Son of Man goes 'just as it is written about Him.' It gives the same table scene as Psalm 41:9 in the Gospel of Matthew and adds the note that the betrayal is both foretold and blameworthy.

The psalmist says it is not an enemy who insults him but 'a man like myself, my companion and close friend,' with whom he shared sweet fellowship. It is the closest Old Testament parallel to Psalm 41:9, and it shows that the treachery of a friend was a wound that David knew from more than one direction.

Absalom sends for 'Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor,' and the conspiracy grows. Ahithophel is the best-known case in David's story of a close adviser turning against him, and readers have long set him beside Psalm 41:9, though the psalm does not name its traitor.

The serpent 'will strike his heel,' using the same noun for heel as Psalm 41:9. The psalm does not quote Genesis, but the heel is the place where the offspring of the woman is wounded by the enemy. The word links the betrayer's hostile act with the first promise of a champion who will suffer and win.

'Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender.' It gives the wisdom principle behind Psalm 41:1-3 in a single line. God takes the care of the weak as a debt to Himself, and in Psalm 41 that repaying takes the form of deliverance and upholding.

The King says of the least of His brothers, 'whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me.' It gives the New Testament weight to Psalm 41:1, by revealing that the weak whom the blessed person considers are ones with whom Christ identifies.

'O LORD my God, I cried to You for help, and You healed me. O LORD, You pulled me up from Sheol.' The testimony of a man healed and raised from the edge of death is the same answer that Psalm 41:3 and 41:10 hope for. Both psalms treat healing as God's gracious answer to a sick man's prayer.

'Against You, You only, have I sinned.' It gives the fuller confession that Psalm 41:4 states briefly. Both texts place sin first and foremost in the relationship with God, and both are set in the mouth of David. The two together show how he prayed when he was ill and when he was guilty.

Paul tells believers not to avenge themselves but to 'leave room for God's wrath' and to 'overcome evil with good.' It shows how the New Testament shapes the wish of Psalm 41:10, 'that I may repay them,' into a call to trust God's justice and to answer evil with good.

Zechariah's song begins 'Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel,' the words that close Psalm 41 and Book I of the Psalter. The Gospel opens with the doxology of the Psalms, and says that God 'has visited and redeemed His people.' The psalm's final praise becomes the first praise of the New Testament.

The doxology at the end of Book II, 'Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel,' with 'Amen and amen,' followed by the note 'Thus conclude the prayers of David.' It shows how the psalter's compilers closed each book with the same kind of praise, so that Psalm 41:13 is read as one of a series.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 41 gathers the theme of Book I, which is the fate of a righteous man in a world that hates him, and gives it a last honest form. The book began with the man who delights in the Law, Psalm 1, and the king who is opposed by the nations and vindicated, Psalm 2. Through David's long run of prayers it shows a servant hunted, sick, slandered and betrayed. Psalm 41 shows that the blessed man is not exempt from these things. He is blessed because in them the LORD holds him, and because the LORD's delight is finally seen.

The betrayal stands in a long line. From the beginning, in Genesis 3, the enemy 'strikes the heel.' Brothers turn on brothers in Genesis 4 and 37, and the covenant people turn on the prophets and on the LORD Himself. When the Lord's anointed is betrayed by a friend, a member of the twelve who ate at His table, the whole line of betrayed righteousness is drawn into one event. In Jesus the words 'lifted up his heel against me' are given their sharpest fulfilment, and the answer to them is not the psalmist's repayment but a raising up, on the third day, that reverses the enemies' claim that 'he will never get up.'

The psalm also sets the vision of a blessed community. Those who care for the weak are the people God backs, and the King they follow is the one who counts the weak as His own. The church's mercy to the poor is one of the marks that the psalm sets before it.

At the end of the story, the enemies are gone, the visitors are truthful, the friends are faithful, and the bed is no more. 'God will wipe away every tear,' and 'there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. The man who prayed to be set before God's face 'forever' has his prayer answered without end, for the redeemed 'will see His face,' Revelation 22:4, and the doxology of Book I, 'from everlasting to everlasting,' is sung without interruption. The double Amen is finally said by a people who have seen the end.

quiz.q: What does the opening beatitude in verses 1-3 promise to the one who cares for the poor?

options.text: The LORD will deliver, protect, preserve, bless, and sustain him, even on his bed of illness.
options.note: This chain of promises links active mercy toward the poor with the LORD's own care in return.

options.text: He will become wealthy immediately as a direct reward.
options.note: The promises concern deliverance, protection, and sustaining care, not an immediate promise of wealth.

options.text: He will never face any trouble at all.
options.note: The text promises deliverance 'in the day of trouble,' implying trouble may come but God will act within it, not that it will never occur.

options.text: He will be exempt from ever needing to confess sin.
options.note: The beatitude concerns caring for the poor; David himself, presumably one who has shown such mercy, still confesses sin in verse 4.

quiz.q: What does David confess about himself in verse 4?

options.text: He asks God to be gracious and heal him, confessing, 'I have sinned against You.'
options.note: David's prayer for healing is joined directly to honest personal confession of sin.

options.text: He claims complete innocence of any wrongdoing.
options.note: The text is an explicit confession of sin, not a claim of innocence.

options.text: He blames his enemies entirely for his illness.
options.note: Verse 4 is personal confession, 'I have sinned against You'; enemies are addressed separately in later verses.

options.text: He refuses to pray about his illness at all.
options.note: Verse 4 is itself a direct prayer for healing, not a refusal to pray.

quiz.q: What happens in verse 9, and how does Jesus use this verse?

options.text: A close, trusted friend who shared his bread betrays him; Jesus quotes this exact verse of Judas's betrayal at the Last Supper, John 13:18.
options.note: This direct New Testament quotation is one of the clearest instances of a psalm verse applied by Jesus to His own experience.

options.text: A stranger David had never met betrays him.
options.note: The verse specifically describes a close, trusted friend, not a stranger, which is what makes the betrayal so sharp.

options.text: Jesus never references this verse anywhere in the Gospels.
options.note: John 13:18 quotes this verse explicitly regarding Judas.

options.text: The betrayal is only symbolic, with no literal act described.
options.note: The text describes a literal act, 'has lifted up his heel against me,' a concrete image of hostile betrayal.

quiz.q: According to verse 11, how does David know that God delights in him?

options.text: Because his enemy does not triumph over him.
options.note: David locates evidence of God's delight in his enemy's failure to prevail, not in the absence of all hardship.

options.text: Because he has never experienced any sickness.
options.note: The psalm explicitly describes David's illness earlier; his confidence in verse 11 concerns his enemy's defeat, not freedom from sickness.

options.text: Because all his friends remained loyal to him.
options.note: Verse 9 describes a close friend's betrayal, so loyalty from all friends is not the basis given for God's delight.

options.text: Because he has become wealthy.
options.note: The stated basis is his enemy's defeat and his own uprightness, not wealth.

quiz.q: How does this psalm close, and what is its significance for the Psalter's structure?

options.text: With the doxology, 'Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Amen and Amen,' closing Book I of the Psalms.
options.note: Each of the Psalter's five books closes with a doxology, and this verse marks the end of Book I, Psalms 1-41.

options.text: With a curse against David's enemies.
options.note: The closing verse is a doxology of praise to God, not a curse against enemies.

options.text: With silence, the psalm simply ending mid-lament.
options.note: The psalm explicitly closes with a full doxology of praise, not an abrupt or silent ending.

options.text: With a promise that David would never face illness again.
options.note: The closing doxology is praise to God's eternal nature, not a specific promise about future illness.

questions: The psalm opens by blessing those who care for the poor. Who is someone poor, sick, or struggling in your life right now that you could actively consider and care for this week?

David prays for healing while honestly confessing, 'I have sinned against You.' Is there a place where you are seeking God's help while avoiding honest confession of what caused or compounds your struggle?

The betrayal by a close friend who shared David's bread is the psalm's sharpest wound. Have you experienced betrayal by someone you deeply trusted, and how does knowing Jesus experienced this exact pattern, quoting this very verse of Judas, meet you in that wound?

David says he knows God delights in him because his enemy does not triumph over him, not because all trouble disappeared. Where in your life might you look for evidence of God's delight in the wrong places?

The psalm closes Book I of the Psalter with unrestrained doxology, even after confessing sin and betrayal. What would it look like for your own prayer life to move toward praise even in the middle of unresolved pain?

translationNotes.note: Poor renders a Hebrew word for the weak, needy, or helpless, and 'considers' implies careful, active attention rather than mere passing awareness.

Bread renders lechem, the staple food symbolizing shared table fellowship and covenant loyalty; 'lifted up his heel' is an idiom for open, contemptuous hostility from someone previously trusted. Jesus quotes this verse directly of Judas in John 13:18.
This doxology closes Book I of the Psalter, Psalms 1-41; each of the Psalter's five books ends with a similar closing blessing.
